title: How would you debug sustained high CPU in a Java service (collect evidence first — CPU metrics, thread dumps, an async/sampling profiler — to find the hot code paths before changing anything), and what are the common causes (tight loops, expensive serialization, lock contention, pathological regex backtracking, and GC pressure)?
shortTitle: How would you debug sustained high CPU in a Java service, and what are the common causes

s1_definition.profdef: Debugging sustained high CPU in a Java service means collecting evidence to locate the exact hot code paths before changing anything. You confirm with CPU metrics per instance, correlate the CPU with the JVM to separate application work from garbage collection, identify which threads are burning CPU, and then use repeated thread dumps or, better, an async or sampling profiler to produce a flame graph that names the hottest methods. Only once the hot path is proven do you fix the root cause, which is typically a tight loop, expensive serialization, lock contention showing as spinning, pathological regular-expression backtracking, or garbage-collection pressure from excessive allocation.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine one teller at National Bank of India is sweating and working furiously non-stop, yet the queue barely moves. A reckless manager would just hire more tellers. A systematic manager watches exactly what that teller is doing over and over: is he re-counting the same stack of notes in an endless loop, is he laboriously re-writing a huge form, is he waiting and fighting with a colleague over a single shared ledger, or is he running out of desk space and constantly cleaning up, which is the garbage-collection equivalent. You observe the busy worker, find the one wasteful task, and fix that specific task. That is how you debug a CPU-bound Java service: profile to see the hot work, then fix it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Debug high CPU by first proving which threads and which methods are burning it with CPU metrics, GC separation, and an async or sampling profiler, then fix the proven cause, usually a tight loop, expensive serialization, lock contention, regex backtracking, or GC pressure.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Debugging sustained high CPU in a Java service means collecting evidence to locate the exact hot code paths before changing anything. You confirm with CPU metrics per instance, correlate the CPU with the JVM to separate application work from garbage collection, identify which threads are burning CPU, and then use repeated thread dumps or, better, an async or sampling profiler to produce a flame graph that names the hottest methods. Only once the hot path is proven do you fix the root cause, which is typically a tight loop, expensive serialization, lock contention showing as spinning, pathological regular-expression backtracking, or garbage-collection pressure from excessive allocation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine one teller at National Bank of India is sweating and working furiously non-stop, yet the queue barely moves. A reckless manager would just hire more tellers. A systematic manager watches exactly what that teller is doing over and over: is he re-counting the same stack of notes in an endless loop, is he laboriously re-writing a huge form, is he waiting and fighting with a colleague over a single shared ledger, or is he running out of desk space and constantly cleaning up, which is the garbage-collection equivalent. You observe the busy worker, find the one wasteful task, and fix that specific task. That is how you debug a CPU-bound Java service: profile to see the hot work, then fix it.

**One line to remember:** Debug high CPU by first proving which threads and which methods are burning it with CPU metrics, GC separation, and an async or sampling profiler, then fix the proven cause, usually a tight loop, expensive serialization, lock contention, regex backtracking, or GC pressure.

sections.s2_technical:
The governing rule is collect evidence before changing anything, because high CPU has several distinct causes and the fix for one is useless or harmful for another, and adding servers to a wasteful code path just burns more money without solving it. You begin by confirming the symptom with CPU metrics per instance over time, checking whether it is all instances or one, and whether it tracks traffic, in which case it may be legitimate load, or stays high even when traffic drops, in which case something is wrong.

The first crucial split is application CPU versus garbage-collection CPU. The JVM can burn CPU either running your code or collecting garbage, and the fixes are opposite. You look at GC metrics and GC logs: if a large fraction of CPU time is spent in GC, with frequent or long collections and the heap repeatedly filling, the cause is GC pressure, usually from excessive allocation, and the fix is to allocate less or size the heap and collector correctly, not to optimise business logic. If GC is quiet, the CPU is genuinely in your code and you proceed to find the hot methods.

To find the hot code you first identify the hot threads, then the hot methods. On Linux you can map operating-system thread CPU usage to Java threads and then take thread dumps to see those threads' stacks; a method that appears RUNNABLE at the top of many dumps a second apart is a hot path. Far better is an async or sampling profiler, such as async-profiler or Java Flight Recorder, which samples stacks cheaply at high frequency and produces a flame graph where the widest bars are exactly where CPU time is spent. The profiler is low overhead and safe to run in production for a short window, and it removes guesswork by naming the hottest methods directly.

Now the common causes, each with its own fingerprint. A tight loop or algorithmic hot spot is a method doing far more work than needed, for example an accidental O(n squared) scan over a growing list, or recomputing something inside a loop that could be computed once; the flame graph shows one business method dominating and the fix is an algorithmic or caching change. Expensive serialization is surprisingly common: converting large objects to and from JSON or another format on every request is CPU-heavy, and the flame graph shows serialization library frames dominating; fixes include serializing less data, reusing mappers, avoiding reflection-heavy paths, or caching serialized forms.

Lock contention shows up when many threads fight for the same lock. CPU can spike because threads spin or because the constant context switching and cache effects waste cycles, and a thread dump shows many threads BLOCKED on the same monitor while one holds it; the fix is to reduce the critical section, use finer-grained or lock-free structures like concurrent collections or atomics, or shard the contended resource. Pathological regular-expression backtracking, often called catastrophic backtracking or regex denial of service, is a classic trap: a poorly written pattern against certain inputs explores an exponential number of match paths, pinning one thread at a hundred percent CPU on a single request; the flame graph shows the regex matcher at the top and the fix is to rewrite the pattern to avoid nested quantifiers, anchor it, or use a non-backtracking engine and input length limits.

GC pressure deserves repeating as a cause of apparent high CPU even when your code looks fine, because heavy short-lived allocation forces constant young-generation collection, and a leak forces repeated full collections; the signature is high GC CPU and allocation rate, and the fix is to allocate less, reuse buffers, avoid boxing in hot paths, and tune the collector and heap.

Senior nuances worth stating: never fix before you measure, because the intuitive culprit is often wrong and the flame graph routinely surprises you; prefer an async or sampling profiler over manual thread dumps because it is both easier and more accurate, and it captures native and GC frames; correlate the onset of high CPU with deploys, config, and input changes, since a new regex or a new serialization path often arrives with a release; capture evidence before restarting, because a restart hides the cause; and remember that high CPU and high latency are different problems, since a service can be slow while CPU is idle, which points instead at waiting on IO, locks, or dependencies.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The fraud-detection service at National Bank of India started pinning every CPU core at a hundred percent and staying there even when traffic dropped, and the team's first instinct was to add more instances. This is exactly the wrong move; the systematic approach is to profile and find the hot method first, because scaling out a wasteful code path just burns more machines.

Problem 2 — GC metrics showed garbage collection was quiet, which meant the CPU was genuinely in application code, not in collection. This is exactly the first split that decides whether you tune allocation or hunt for a hot method.

Problem 3 — A flame graph showed almost all CPU time inside the regular-expression matcher used to validate transaction narration text, caused by a pattern with nested quantifiers hitting a crafted long input, which is catastrophic backtracking. This is exactly regex-driven high CPU, and the fix is to rewrite the pattern and bound the input, not to add servers.

Our mini-project builds a tiny CPU-diagnostics harness. The code runs two workloads, a healthy one and a pathological-regex one, measures CPU-like busy time, and prints a simplified hot-method summary from sampled stacks, so you can see the regex matcher dominate. It also demonstrates a tight-loop hot path for contrast. The demo investigates high CPU while validating transaction narrations for Rajesh and Priya.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the CPU diagnostics harness
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/cpu/CpuDiagnosticsDemo.java
java -cp target/classes com.bank.cpu.CpuDiagnosticsDemo

# Real production tooling to find hot code paths:
async-profiler -d 30 -e cpu -f flame.html <pid>   # CPU flame graph
jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=rec.jfr # Java Flight Recorder
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000                           # confirm GC is NOT the cause
top -H -p <pid>                                    # per-thread CPU (map TID to Java thread)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a crafted transaction narration, the string "Rajesh salary" followed by thirty letters and an exclamation mark, validated fifty times, run through a service whose CPU is pinned.

Step 1: First the engineer confirms CPU is high and stays high even as traffic falls, then checks GC. GC is quiet, so the CPU is genuinely in application code. This split tells the team to hunt for a hot method rather than tune allocation.

Step 2: The sampling profiler starts, taking a stack sample every few milliseconds of the busy thread. The bad workload runs: fifty validations using the pattern with nested quantifiers. Each validation against the crafted input forces the regex engine to explore an exploding number of match paths, so a single call can take a long time and burns CPU the whole time.

Step 3: The profiler accumulates samples, and because the thread spends almost all its time inside the regex matcher, the overwhelming majority of samples land on the matcher's methods. When the profiler prints its hot-method summary, the regex matcher is at the top by a wide margin, exactly like the widest bar in a flame graph. This names the culprit without guessing.

Step 4: The evidence points to catastrophic backtracking in the narration validator. The fix is twofold: rewrite the pattern to remove the nested quantifier so matching is linear, and bound the input length so even a bad pattern cannot blow up. The code switches to the safe pattern with a length check.

Step 5: The same fifty validations run with the safe pattern and complete almost instantly, and the CPU returns to normal. The before-and-after timing proves the fix: the bad workload took a large number of milliseconds while the safe one is near zero, confirming the regex was the cause.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:11:00 INFO    GC quiet → CPU is in application code, profile to find hot method
2026-10-24 15:11:04 SEVERE  BAD regex validated 50 narrations in 4120ms (CPU pinned)
2026-10-24 15:11:04 SEVERE  HOT METHODS (by sample count, widest = hottest):
2026-10-24 15:11:04 SEVERE     780 samples  java.util.regex.Pattern$Curly.match
2026-10-24 15:11:04 SEVERE     42 samples  com.bank.cpu.NarrationValidator.isValidBad
2026-10-24 15:11:04 INFO    SAFE regex validated 50 narrations in 3ms (CPU normal)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To debug sustained high CPU in a Java service I collect evidence before touching anything, because high CPU has several distinct causes whose fixes are different, and scaling out a wasteful code path just burns more machines without solving it. I confirm the symptom with CPU metrics per instance and check whether it tracks traffic, which can be legitimate load, or stays high when traffic falls, which means something is wrong.

My first split is application CPU versus garbage-collection CPU, because the fixes are opposite. I look at GC metrics and logs: if a large share of CPU is in collection with the heap repeatedly filling, the cause is GC pressure from excessive allocation and I fix allocation and heap sizing, not business logic. If GC is quiet, the CPU is genuinely in my code, so I find the hot threads and then the hot methods, ideally with an async or sampling profiler like async-profiler or Java Flight Recorder, which samples stacks cheaply and produces a flame graph whose widest bars name the hottest methods. It is low overhead, safe for a short production window, and removes guesswork.

Then I match the flame graph to the common causes, each with a fingerprint. A tight loop or bad algorithm shows one business method dominating. Expensive serialization shows JSON or mapper frames on top and is fixed by serializing less, reusing mappers, and caching. Lock contention shows many threads blocked on one monitor in a thread dump and is fixed by shrinking the critical section or using lock-free structures. Catastrophic regex backtracking shows the regex matcher pinning a core on a single request and is fixed by rewriting the pattern to avoid nested quantifiers and bounding input length. And GC pressure, again, shows high GC CPU and allocation rate rather than business frames.

On my project at National Bank of India the fraud-detection service pinned every core and stayed pinned even when traffic dropped, and the team wanted to add instances. We resisted, confirmed GC was quiet, ran a profiler, and the flame graph put almost all CPU inside the regular-expression matcher used to validate transaction narration, caused by a pattern with nested quantifiers hitting a crafted long input, which is classic catastrophic backtracking. We rewrote the pattern to be linear and bounded the input length, and the validation that had taken seconds dropped to milliseconds with CPU back to normal. The lessons I stress are to never fix before I measure because the intuitive culprit is usually wrong, to prefer a sampling profiler over manual thread dumps, to correlate the onset with deploys and new inputs, to capture evidence before restarting, and to remember that high CPU and high latency are different problems, since a slow service with idle CPU is a waiting problem, not a computing one.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I debug high CPU by proving which threads and methods burn it, first splitting application CPU from GC and then using an async or sampling profiler to read the flame graph, and only then fixing the proven cause, which is almost always a tight loop, expensive serialization, lock contention, regex backtracking, or GC pressure.
